title: The Battery Line Wang Chuanfu Built by Hand Instead of Buying
dek: In late 1994 Wang Chuanfu could not afford a Japanese automated battery line, so his new company broke one into steps people could do by hand.

story.event: Building BYD's first nickel battery line from manual steps and fixtures instead of buying Japanese automation
story.summary: In November 1994 Wang Chuanfu, a chemist who had left a state research institute, began work in Shenzhen with a team of 20 on a battery company licensed early in 1995 as BYD, with some $300,000 raised from relatives. Unable to afford automated Japanese production lines or get a bank loan, the team broke the process into manual steps done with fixtures and home-built equipment, hiring workers where Japanese factories used robots. By 2002 BYD ranked among the world's top four makers of each main type of rechargeable battery, supplying Motorola and Nokia.
paragraphs: On 18 November 1994, Wang Chuanfu led a team of 20 to work in Shenzhen on a battery business that did not yet legally exist; its licence, he recalled thirty years later, came only in early 1995. Wang, a chemist, had studied and worked at a state research institute in Beijing. He told BusinessWeek in 2003 that he had hoped for a quiet research career, "My target was to be a very good engineer," but government laboratories had too little money to do much.

He could see a market. The brick-sized mobile phones of the day ran on nickel batteries, and owners often bought a spare or two. Most came from Japan, and importing them, he told Fortune, meant duties and long waits for delivery. Relatives and friends warned him that leaving a secure state job with no resources or connections was too risky. He left anyway, with some $300,000 that, Fortune reported, he raised from relatives.

The obvious way to make nickel batteries was to buy an automated production line from Japan. "We didn't have much money in our pockets and couldn't afford it," Wang said later, and with few assets to pledge, no bank would lend. So the team studied the automated process, broke it into steps a person could do by hand with the help of fixtures, and built much of the equipment themselves. Wang also pored over Sony's and Sanyo's patents and took batteries apart to see how they were made. Where Japanese lines used robotic arms costing $100,000 or more each, BYD hired people, first hundreds, then thousands. To keep quality steady, every job was cut into basic tasks with strict testing. Wang put the cost of the whole first line at a quarter to a fifth of a Japanese one.

By 2002, according to a Harvard Business School case cited by Fortune, BYD was among the world's top four makers of each of the three main kinds of rechargeable battery, and that year it listed in Hong Kong with Motorola and Nokia as customers. The approach rested on the migrant workers who filled Shenzhen's factories; Fortune reported in 2009 that they typically earned about $190 a month. In 2003 Wang bought a nearly defunct state-owned car maker, a move that startled investors.

quote.text: Of course man is useful to man, because his body is a marvellous machine and his mind an organ of wonderful efficiency.  But he is a spirit as well, and this spirit is truly known only by love.
quote.source_title: Sadhana: The Realisation of Life, Project Gutenberg eBook #6842
quote.connection: BYD's breakthrough was a sum: people cost less than robots, and could be organised to work as precisely. Tagore does not deny that bodies and minds are useful. He insists usefulness is the smaller truth about a person. The sum and his warning can both hold, and the second is easiest to forget when the first is working.

reflection: When the proper equipment is out of reach, it is tempting to treat the gap as a reason to wait. Wang's team treated it as a question: what does the machine actually do, one step at a time, and which of those steps can a careful person do instead?

Tagore adds what the costing leaves out. When a plan of yours leans on someone's hours, a colleague covering a shift, someone at home taking on more so you can work late, those hours are not free just because nobody sends a bill. Making do is often wise. It is fairer when you can name who is carrying it.
invitation: Choose one task you have been postponing until you can afford a better tool. Write its steps on paper, and circle one step you could do by hand this week.

cross_checks.claim: Wang founded BYD in Shenzhen, with work starting in late 1994 and the company licensed in early 1995
He started with some $300,000 (about 2.5 million yuan) raised from relatives
Instead of buying automated Japanese lines, BYD broke production into manual steps and hired workers where rivals used robots
By 2002 BYD was among the world's leading rechargeable battery makers and listed in Hong Kong, with Motorola and Nokia among its customers
In 2003 Wang moved BYD into car-making by buying a struggling state-owned car company

research_notes: Founding date: most reports say 1995; in his 30th-anniversary speech (18 November 2024) Wang dated the start of work to 18 November 1994 with a team of 20, the licence following early in 1995, so the story gives both. Start-up money: Fortune (2009) says some $300,000 from relatives; China Daily via Gasgoo (2010) says 2.5 million yuan, which matches at mid-1990s exchange rates; CNN (2009) says capital from 'a relative'; Wikipedia says his cousin Lu Xiangyang lent 250,000 yuan, citing the CNN piece, which gives no such figure; CnEVPost (2020, unsigned, not cited) gives both '$2.5 million' and '3 million'. The story uses Fortune's $300,000 from relatives, which the China Daily figure corroborates; the Gasgoo reprint of China Daily loads only intermittently, so the story does not depend on it alone. Market position: CNN says BYD was the world's biggest phone-battery maker by 2000, Fortune 'one of the world's largest' by about 2000, BusinessWeek (2003) 'among the top three makers of high-end rechargeable batteries', and Wang (2024) that its nickel battery sales became the world's number one; the story uses Fortune's citation of the Harvard Business School case (top four in each of three technologies by 2002) as the conservative figure. The 'quarter to a fifth' line cost is Wang's own figure and is attributed to him. The 36Kr text is an English translation of a Chinese speech, so the short quotation is the translation's wording. The $190 monthly wage is Fortune's 2009 figure for Shenzhen migrant factory workers generally ('in vast factories like those run by BYD'), not a BYD payroll figure, and the story says so. Fortune and CNN were both Time Warner titles in 2009; the labour-for-robots decision is also supported by Wang's own speech and CarNewsChina. The Fortune and BusinessWeek pages are cited from Internet Archive copies because the live URLs return errors. The Tagore passage is from his chapter on love, where he warns against valuing people only by the service they render; it is applied here by analogy and implies no judgement of BYD beyond what the sources report.
